summary: Terminating decimals and fractions are two notations for one value, with percentages a third. A terminating decimal is read by its LAST place value to get a power-of-ten denominator (0.375 = 375/1000), then simplified (= 3/8). Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125). The deep idea: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (the primes of ten); any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) makes it recur. Learners should both convert fluently in both directions AND predict termination from the denominator's prime factorisation, not by dividing and guessing.
misconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors

activities.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
steps: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
activities.insight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.

activities.title: Read a decimal by its last place value
steps: Name the place value of the LAST digit of 0.375 (thousandths), so the starting denominator is 1000: write 0.375 = 375/1000.
Simplify stepwise to lowest terms: 375/1000 = 3/8 (divide both by 125). Check the simplified fraction against the original decimal.
Repeat with other decimals (0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5; 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4; 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20), each time naming the last place value first.
Reverse the direction: convert 3/8 to a decimal two ways — divide 3 ÷ 8, and scale 3/8 to 375/1000 — and confirm both give 0.375.
activities.insight: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator; reading the last place value gives that denominator, and simplifying gives lowest terms. Fraction→decimal is division (numerator ÷ denominator), equivalently scaling to a power of ten.

activities.title: Sort, match and fill the gaps (consolidation)
steps: Match terminating decimals to their simplest fractions: 0.375 ↔ 3/8, 0.2 ↔ 1/5, 0.25 ↔ 1/4.
Sort a set of fractions into two columns, 'terminates' and 'recurs', by inspecting each denominator's prime factors (not by dividing): e.g. 7/40 and 1/20 terminate; 5/12 and 1/6 recur.
Fill in the chain 0.375 = __/1000 = __/8, then explain each step (last place value → denominator, then the ÷125 simplification).

Transfer to unfamiliar fractions: predict whether 9/25, 4/15 and 6/15 terminate, justify from the prime factors of each denominator in lowest terms (6/15 = 2/5), then check by converting (9/25 = 0.36; 4/15 = 0.2666…; 6/15 = 0.4).
activities.insight: Bidirectional conversion to simplest form becomes fluent, and the terminate/recur judgement is made from the denominator's prime factors rather than by trial division.

activities.title: Predict and justify: will it stop? (optional discussion)
steps: Before converting, predict aloud whether a given fraction (e.g. 1/6, 7/40, 5/12) terminates or recurs, and say WHY from the denominator.
Justify the prediction by naming the prime factors of the denominator and relating them to the primes of ten (2 and 5).
Have a partner or adult pose the question 'How could you know without doing the whole division?' and respond with a reasoned argument, then check by converting.
activities.insight: Verbalising the prediction and its reason is intended to reveal whether the learner reasons from structure (prime factors) or merely from procedures; articulating the reason aims to strengthen the conceptual link, though that effect is not established here.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Convert 0.375 to a fraction in its simplest form, and convert 3/8 to a decimal. Then tell me — will 1/6 give a decimal that stops, or one that goes on forever? How could you know without doing the whole division?' Watch how they work and listen to the reason for 1/6.
checkAnswer: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (dividing by 125); 3/8 = 0.375 (3 ÷ 8, or ×125 to make 375/1000). 1/6 does NOT stop — 6 = 2×3, and the factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so it recurs (0.1666…).
